# Voxelization via Rasterization
## Overview
This family generates a voxel representation of 3D geometry by projecting input primitives onto 2D planes, rasterizing them for coverage, and mapping the results to 3D voxel coordinates [S1, unofficial]. It distinguishes itself from siblings like [Binary Volume Rendering](1015-binary-volume-rendering-opacity-thresholding.md) and [Naive Voxel Rendering](1103-naive-voxel-rendering.md) by leveraging established 2D rasterization pipelines instead of brute-force 3D traversal or simple thresholding [G].
## Shared principles

## Subtopics

### [3-axis rasterization voxelization](2480-3-axis-rasterization-voxelization.md)
Produces a 6-separating voxelization of 3D input geometry by rasterizing primitives along three axis-aligned projection directions in three separate passes. It is distinct from 26-separating methods by generating a sparser voxel set sufficient for applications using 6-connected ray marching. It is equivalent to using a "crosshairs" intersection target and is notably robust for curved primitives, requiring only point-depth evaluations. Choose this method when a sparse, 6-connected voxel boundary is required [G].

### [Chunked UV Rasterization with Face ID Storage](2598-chunked-uv-rasterization-with-face-id-storage.md)
Rasterizes a 3D mesh in 2D UV space to generate voxel data, using memory-friendly chunking to handle large geometries. It differs from [3-axis rasterization voxelization](2480-3-axis-rasterization-voxelization.md) by projecting onto a single UV plane per pass and storing face identifiers to enable precise 3D position interpolation, rather than relying on depth buffers or multiple axis projections. It addresses VRAM limitations by processing faces in batches. Choose this method for large meshes where VRAM is limited and precise surface position interpolation is needed [G].

### [Triangle Projection Voxelization](5432-triangle-projection-voxelization.md)
Converts a triangle mesh into a voxel grid by rasterizing triangles using a union-based approach to resolve overlaps and coverage. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly combining multiple passes or render targets to ensure correct voxel coverage. Choose this method when a direct GPU-based voxelization with overlap resolution is required [G].

### [DX11.1 Forced Sample Count Optimization](8063-dx11-1-forced-sample-count-optimization.md)

### Conservative Rasterization via Edge Expansion
**Definition:** A technique to fix 'holes' introduced by switching projection directions in different primitives [S1, unofficial]. Standard rasterization invokes the pixel shader only if a primitive covers the pixel center; this method expands primitive edges to ensure all pixels touched by the primitive are covered [S1, unofficial].
**Step:** Expand primitive edges in the Geometry Shader to ensure all pixels touched by the primitive are covered by the rasterizer [S1, unofficial].
**Pitfall:** Edge expansion causes extra pixels to be shaded, particularly for thin triangles, leading to unnecessary pixel shader calls [S1, unofficial]. These extra voxels must be culled later using voxel-primitive intersection tests [S1, unofficial].

### Hardware Conservative Rasterization
**Definition:** Using hardware-supported conservative rasterization available on Maxwell base chipsets or higher via NVAPI [S1, unofficial]. It avoids artifacts from manual edge expansion and eliminates the need for subsequent voxel-primitive intersection tests [S1, unofficial].
**Parameter:** Hardware Requirement: Maxwell base chip set or higher [S1, unofficial].
**Comparison:** Unlike manual edge expansion, hardware conservative rasterization does not produce extra shaded pixels, so voxel-primitive intersection tests are not needed [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The technique originates from NVIDIA's GPU voxelization research, which leverages the maturity and speed of 2D graphics pipelines to solve 3D geometric problems [S1, unofficial]. It avoids the computational overhead of explicit 3D intersection tests [G]. The specific variants within this family have been developed to address limitations in memory usage (chunking), connectivity requirements (6-axis vs 26-axis), and overlap resolution (union-based hashing) [G].
